17. One expression, many engines

If you've ever moved a query from one engine to another and watched a number change, this appendix is the long version of why. A query or an Ibis expression has no single meaning: each engine gives it its own. This notebook collects the questions that a semantics written from first principles (instead of read off one implementation) has to answer, and shows how each engine answers them today. It is the companion of chapter 16, which compares DataFusion alone with the Lean model. Every entry is one small question, such as "what is -7 % 2?" or "where do NULLs go in a descending sort?". It is asked three ways, and every answer except Snowflake's is computed live when the notebook runs:
  • Native engines. The SQL runs on DataFusion and DuckDB, and the Polars expression runs on Polars. Snowflake is quoted from its documentation, since there is no account to run on. The SQL standard is given in prose where it says something.
  • Ibis. One Ibis expression, executed by Ibis's DataFusion, DuckDB and Polars backends. The Snowflake SQL that Ibis compiles it to is under "Snowflake SQL". Ibis promises one meaning for one expression, and this column tests that promise.
  • Lean and sverify. Rel.eval of the plan that DataFusion makes from the SQL (Lean prints doubles with a d, ±0.0 as their codes ±1, and timestamps as microseconds). Then the plan Lean writes back out (written_plan), run by sverify's own translators to Polars and DuckDB, plus whether the Snowflake and Spark SQL generators accept it (chapter 11 runs the Spark SQL on a real Spark session). These translators are meant to reproduce Rel.eval exactly, whatever the native engine would do.
Each entry gets three tags:
  • engines: uniform if the native engines agree, split if they don't. A split entry is a decision a formal semantics must make explicitly.
  • Ibis: portable if the Ibis expression gives the same result on every backend, leaky if the backend shows through. This tag is computed live (comparing results as bags) and is blank when no Ibis backend runs the expression.
  • sverify: faithful if both translators give Lean's answer (or fail where Lean says a runtime error is possible), refused if the checker or a translator rejects the plan, opaque if Lean leaves the function uninterpreted and the translators disagree, and GAP if a translator is wrong.
sverify verifies an Ibis expression by compiling it to DataFusion's SQL, so the meaning sverify checks is the one Ibis-on-DataFusion gives it. Wherever the Ibis tag is leaky, running the same expression on another Ibis backend can break what was proved.

Summary

Built from the catalogue below. First, the entries where sverify itself is wrong or undetermined, then the Ibis expressions whose meaning depends on the backend, and last the questions the engines answer differently, each with the answer the Lean model gives today.

Setup

One tiny table per topic, put into DataFusion (through sverify), DuckDB and Polars, and given to Ibis as a memtable. Lean gets the same rows, inlined into the plan as a Substrait virtual table. DataFusion gets the tables as they are (put_table would store them the model's way, with one zero and one NaN), so its native answers show its own order.

1. NULL and three-valued logic

SQL has three truth values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN (written NULL). A comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, and a filter keeps a row only when its condition is TRUE. AND and OR follow Kleene's tables: FALSE AND NULL is FALSE, but TRUE AND NULL is NULL. Every engine agrees on that core. The differences are in what the surface languages, Ibis and Polars, choose to mean by ==, isin and friends.

2. Order: NULL placement, row numbers and window frames

A table is a bag of rows: it has no order until ORDER BY gives it one, and even then rows with equal keys (ties) may come out in any order. Where NULLs go in a sort is a convention. The SQL standard leaves it to the implementation, but it must be consistent: NULLs sort either above or below every value. Window functions add frames: which rows a running SUM adds up. The standard's default frame when there is an ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE means rows tied with the current one (its peers) are included.

3. Integers

Mathematical integers are unbounded, while engines store them in 64 bits (BIGINT, values from −2⁶³ to 2⁶³ − 1). The questions are what / and % mean on integers, what happens at the edges (division by zero, overflow), and what a cast does. "Truncating" division rounds toward zero (−7 / 2 = −3); "floor" division rounds down (−7 // 2 = −4). The remainder follows: truncating gives −7 % 2 = −1, floor gives +1.

4. Doubles and rounding

IEEE 754 doubles have two zeros (+0.0 and −0.0, equal under IEEE =) and NaN ("not a number", unequal to everything, itself included, under IEEE =). Databases cannot use IEEE = as is, because GROUP BY and DISTINCT need an equality where every value equals itself. So each engine picks its own fix, and the fixes differ. Rounding a half (2.5) also has two common conventions: half away from zero (2.5 → 3, −2.5 → −3) and half to even, also called banker's rounding (2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4).

A string is a sequence of something: bytes (UTF-8), Unicode code points, or grapheme clusters (what a reader sees as one character). 6. Aggregates

An aggregate folds a column into one value. Two conventions matter: SQL aggregates (except COUNT) skip NULLs and return NULL when nothing is left, and COUNT(DISTINCT x) does not count NULL as a value. Lean verifies aggregates, and sverify's translators run them with its semantics. Snowflake's SQL refuses a double SUM or AVG over a named table, whose result depends on the order rows are added in.

data.text/markdown:
What this means for a formal semantics

  • Pick, don't inherit. Of the questions above, the split ones have no engine-neutral answer. The Lean model mostly takes DataFusion's, which made sense while DataFusion was the only engine. A semantics of its own would state each choice (truncating division, −0.0 < +0.0, NULL as the largest value, 1-based positions) and treat every engine as something to translate into, as sverify's Polars and DuckDB translators already do.
  • Ibis is a language of its own. Its expressions do not mean the SQL they compile to: == null is IS NULL, row_number and find and substr are 0-based, sorts put NULLs last in both directions, and a window with an order_by but no frame covers the whole partition. And where Ibis does not normalise (%, round, cast, length, nunique, max with NaN, like), the backend shows through. A semantics of Ibis expressions should therefore be defined on Ibis's own operations, with sverify checking against Ibis-on-DataFusion only as one implementation.
  • Uninterpreted is not the same as agreed. upper, lower and regular expressions are black boxes in Lean, which keeps proofs honest, and sverify's translators used to compute them with different Unicode tables (S4, S6). Their meaning is now pinned to Rust's str::to_uppercase and regex crate (DataFusion, Polars); the SQL translations raise on non-ASCII text where their engines could differ, so "the same plan, the same rows, or an error" holds across engines.
  • sverify gaps found here, all fixed. Constant casts used to round (CAST(2.7 AS BIGINT) was proved to be 3; DataFusion gives 2, F9) and to trim spaces from strings (' 12' was proved to be 12; DataFusion fails, S8); constants now fold by the same rules as columns, and strings DataFusion cannot parse are refused. Narrowing casts were the identity (I10, chapter 16's I8); they are now range-checked and may raise badCast. The Polars translator crashed on duplicate output column names (N4); it now keeps them.
python/tests/test_backend_semantics.py pins the native behaviours that sverify's translators work around (Polars' floor %, NULL on division by zero and NULLs-first sort, DuckDB's double /, IEEE zeros and half-to-even cast, and so on), so an upgrade that changes one of them shows up, and pins each fixed gap so that it stays fixed.
